text: Last week, Sparks of Weight-Space Programming by Takehi et al. at MIT CSAIL caught our eye: it had one language model improve another by editing its weights directly, with no training run and no gradients. If such a mechanism were to hold up, a model could fix another model the way it already fixes a prompt or code, which is a step toward continual learning driven by models themselves. Its headline result: GPT-6 Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B, a small model that runs out of thinking tokens on 93% of MATH-500 problems, mostly mid-loop, and lifted its accuracy from 7.9% to 48.1%. We gave the same task to Beaker , our autonomous agent improver. In about an hour, Beaker found a one-neuron edit that cuts loops and raises accuracy by 30 points. Qwen3.5-0.8B gets most math problems wrong because it hits its token limit before giving an answer, usually while stuck repeating lines that start with "Wait". Beaker traced the loops to a single neuron using only the weights and the scored answers of its edits, without running the model. Doubling that neuron's output lifted MATH-500 accuracy from 7.4% to 37.4%. When we analyzed the changes, we found that the neuron Beaker identified lowers the probability that the model writes "Wait". By doubling its output, Beaker reduced that probability further, allowing the model to get out of loops more often. What else Beaker found: The idea is simple: instead of training a network, a language model reads its weights and writes new values directly. 1 Takehi et al. gave GPT-6 Astra a CPU Python session with the weights and a budget of GPU passes. Each pass runs the model once on a batch Astra picks: it can either generate answers with Astra's current edit, or run texts through the model to read its activations. We call this access reads + generation. Two experiments set the scene for ours: In this post we investigate four questions: Beaker autonomously runs experiments to improve agents. It works in rounds: Beaker suggests a change, scores it on training cases (labeled examples with known answers), and keeps it only if the gain beats measured noise, repeating until it stops finding measurable improvements. The final result is reported on held-out cases Beaker never sees. For these experiments, Beaker edits the model's weights ( Figure 1 ). We ran Beaker two ways: In both, Beaker builds a checkpoint for every edit, scores it on 256 training cases (128 GSM8K, 128 MATH) and keeps it only if it beats measured noise. MATH-500 is held out and run with Takehi et al.'s settings. 4 Reproduction. The unedited model scored 6.2–8.4% across our runs, against their 7.9%. Their edit, rebuilt bit for bit from its published diff , scored 51.1% in our harness against their 48.1%. All numbers below are ours except Takehi et al.'s 25-pass result (14.1%). The completed math runs, with and without model reads, best first: Neuron numbers count the neurons of one layer's MLP, and neurons with no layer named are in layer 22. "×2" means a neuron's output column was doubled, and "+ gate" or "− gate" means a copy of its gate row, as long as its up row, was added to or subtracted from its up row, so the neuron's output grows faster as its gate opens. Four of these five runs found neuron 573. Combined, Beaker's edits reach 43.0%. Between them, these runs found nine different neuron edits. Applied together, they lift MATH-500 from 8.2% to 43.0%, against 36.6% for neuron 573 ×2 alone in the same harness. Where runs edited the same neuron (neuron 573 in four runs, neuron 387 in two), we kept the edit from the best run: The extra gain over neuron 573 alone comes from fewer answers cut off at the token limit (50%, against 62%). The answers that do finish are right a little less often (85%, against 93%). Interestingly, neuron 573 alone accounts for about four-fifths of the combined gain over the unedited model's 8.2%, which warrants a closer look at the role it plays and how Beaker identified it. To better understand what neuron 573 does, let's start by looking at how a layer contributes to the model's output. At each position in the text, Qwen3.5-0.8B carries one vector of 1,024 numbers, the residual stream. 5 The token's row of the embedding matrix starts it off. Each of the 24 layers reads the vector and adds its own output to it. Only attention moves information between positions; the MLP works on each position's vector on its own. At the top, after a final norm, the model scores every token in its vocabulary by a dot product with each position's vector, and the highest scores are the likeliest tokens to come after that position. In symbols, at one position in one layer: x is the residual stream and x ˆ its normalized copy. W gate and W up are 3,584 × 1,024 matrices and W down is 1,024 × 3,584. How strongly each neuron fires is one entry of the vector h : where SiLU is a smooth switch that stays near zero for negative inputs and ⊙ multiplies entry by entry. The layer then adds every neuron's output column, scaled by how strongly it fired; h i is neuron i 's activation and w i its column of W down : So changing one column from w i to w i + Δ w adds h i Δ w to the stream at every position, in proportion to how strongly that neuron fires there: The edit our runs found doubles the output column of neuron 573 in layer 22's MLP ( Figure 3 ): 1,024 numbers, about a millionth of the model. In the formula above that is Δ w = w 573 , so the neuron's push doubles wherever it fires (the close-up in Figure 3 ). Just before "Wait", neuron 573 fires negative. Its column points toward "Wait", as we show from the weights below ( Figure 4 ), so the layer subtracts it: that lowers the stream's dot product with "Wait", the score the output layer uses, and makes "Wait" less likely. Takehi et al.'s edit, covered below, changes 64 columns per layer instead of one. Each neuron fires with some strength. Beaker found neuron 573 with both models. The first run to find it, with Sol, never ran the model. It started from the scored answers: every failed answer had run out of tokens mid-thought, and most were stuck repeating lines that restart with "Wait". So it searched the weights for neurons that control "Wait". The weights alone are enough for that search because Qwen3.5 uses weight tying. The embedding table, a 248,320 × 1,024 matrix with one row per token, does two jobs: the first is to turn each input token into the starting value of its position's stream, the second is to score every possible next token. For the second, the model multiplies the table by the final stream at a position (after the final norm): each token's score is the dot product of its row with that stream, and a softmax turns the 248,320 scores into next-token probabilities. So the " Wait" row plays both parts. Wherever the input token is " Wait", the stream at that position starts as this row, and the score of " Wait" as the next token is this row's dot product with the final stream. This means you can read a neuron's effect on "Wait" directly from the weights: the more its output column points along the " Wait" row, the more its firing moves the score of "Wait". For every MLP neuron in all 24 layers, Beaker measured how closely its output column points along tokens like " Wait", "Therefore" and </think> . Neuron 573 in layer 22 stood out, and its gate and up rows line up with " Wait" too ( Figure 4 ). Beaker read this as a built-in brake on "Wait" and doubled the column once, without trying other strengths. Its score on the 256 training cases went from 10.5% to 46.1%. Weakening the column floods the thinking with "Wait" and accuracy collapses below 2%. Doubling it removes "Wait" and lifts accuracy to 36.6%; stronger multipliers plateau ( Figure 5 ). A plain token ban does the same job. To ban a token, we lower its score before each token is sampled: for t = " Wait" (with a leading space) and t = "Wait", the logit ℓ t becomes ℓ t − 100 . After the softmax, that token's probability drops to at most e − 100 times what it was, so it is never sampled, and the other tokens split its share in proportion to their own probabilities. The weights and the prompt stay the same. This ban scores 37.6%. That is within noise of doubling the column (+0.9 ± 1.1), and the two solve almost the same problems. So the most-found edit is a token ban, found by reading weights: it fixes one habit rather than adding math ability. Takehi et al.'s edit works in three steps, done separately in layers 15 and 19: In symbols, with u the repetition direction (length 1) and w j one of the chosen columns: The part along u goes from ( u · w j ) to − 5 × ( u · w j ) . These neurons fire on almost every token, so the edit adds roughly the same push toward wrapping up everywhere, whether or not the model is looping. A recent analysis tested this directly. It left the weights alone and simply added a fixed push along the same direction to layers 15 and 19 at every token, and got the same gain: 50.8% on MATH-500, against 50.0% for the edit itself in its tests. The direction is unrelated to "Wait", which is why the "Wait" ban stacks on top ( Figure 6 ). Before the edit, these neurons push slightly toward looping. Takehi et al.'s edit took GPT-6 Astra about 10 hours of work and 50 passes, and changed 131,072 numbers. Its run lasted 20 hours, but the same analysis found in their logs that 4.7 of those hours were an outage and the last passes only re-tested a finished edit. Our best Beaker run took 8 hours and changed 3 output columns (3,072 numbers). Our run without model reads found its edit, a single column (1,024 numbers), in its first hour; the run lasted 4 hours. Takehi et al.'s edit still scores higher in our harness, and half of it plus the "Wait" ban scores higher still ( Figure 7 ). The ban doesn't stop looping; it changes the loop. With "Wait" banned, 6 in 10 answers still run out of tokens, now repeating lines that start with "So", "If" or "Let's". We checked loops on a quarter of MATH-500 (125 problems), counting an answer as stuck when it repeats the same line 5 or more times. 7 The two edits deal with loops in opposite ways ( Figure 8 ): Net effect: on those 125 problems, 62 in 100 answers finish with Takehi et al.'s edit, against 37 with the ban. Across all 500 problems, it gets more right overall (51% against 38%), mostly by finishing hard problems that used to run out of tokens. Layer 15 does the work. We split the edit into its two halves and ran each with and without the "Wait" ban (the " Wait" and "Wait" tokens blocked while the model writes; no prompt or weight change): Layer 15 alone keeps most loops finishing and loses only 4.3 ± 1.0 points against the full edit; layer 19 alone is weaker than the plain ban. With the ban on, layer 19 adds nothing: layer 15 plus the ban scores 58.7%, and on the hardest MATH level it nearly doubles the ban alone (31.0% against 16.6%). So Takehi et al.'s 131,072-number edit comes down to one direction in 64 neurons of layer 15, plus a one-line decoding rule. One stops a common loop from starting; the other gets the model out of loops it falls into anyway. Takehi et al. only asked for higher scores on fixed tasks: math accuracy, game points. Beaker can take any goal it can score. It runs the same loop as before: propose an edit, score it on training cases, keep it only if the score rises beyond noise, and repeat. The score is the only thing that tells it what we want. So we wrote scores for two behaviors Takehi et al. didn't try, on the same 0.8B model with thinking off, and let Beaker search the weights for each. We chose the goals and wrote the scores; Beaker chose and tested the edits. These runs had reads + generation: 20 passes per round, each either a read or a batch of answers the model generated to prompts that Beaker chose (never the scored cases). The goal: keep the model's answers as short as its own "answer briefly" version, without a prompt. How the score works. For every question we first record two answers from the unedited model, with the same random seed: its normal answer and its answer when told to "answer briefly". Each answer from an edited model then earns: The score is the average over all held-out questions. The unedited model's 0.26 comes mostly from the 150-word requests (0.20 of it), which are a fifth of the questions. The result: all three runs kept edits, raising the held-out score from 0.26 to 0.355 (Astra), 0.341 and 0.327 (Sol), and making answers a third to a half shorter. Factual answers held up, and requests for long answers were still honored. Math and open answers lost accuracy, much as they do when the model is simply told to be brief: the edit reproduces the instruction, cost included. The edits: each run's main edit took three steps. First, it compared the model's internal state with and without "Answer briefly." in the prompt; the difference is a "be brief" direction, the change that instruction makes inside the model. Next, it found a neuron that fires mostly as an answer begins. Last, it wrote the "be brief" direction into that neuron's output column, so whenever an answer starts, the neuron adds part of the change the instruction would have made, with no instruction in the prompt ( Figure 9 ). Our instructions passed on this approach from earlier runs; each run chose its own neurons and strengths. Different runs often picked the same neurons: layer 14 neuron 2172, layer 19 neuron 847 and layer 15 neuron 2242 each turned up twice. Before the edit, these neurons barely push the model toward a brief answer. The score (brevity credit, given only to right answers) rose for every kind of question except requests for long answers, and answers got a third to a half shorter: Correctness on its own fell. Math answers right dropped from 80% to 23–54%, and open answers accepted by the judge from 30% to 11–18%. Factual answers held up: a loose check (right answer named anywhere) fell from 81% to 61–80%, but 47–54% still give the right answer in the first sentence, against 49% unedited. The loose factual check drops because unedited answers are long, and many pass only because they name the right answer somewhere after a wrong or hedged first guess. Edited answers stop after that first guess, so the check now catches it. Not every drop is like this, though: in the Sol run that scored 0.341, we estimate that 7 of the 19 points it lost are answers that really went wrong. There are real math losses. Short math answers skip the working and then get the answer wrong more often, just as they do when you simply ask the model to be brief (GSM8K accuracy fell from 46% to 0% in our pre-check). The score also misses some side effects. For example, one run starts every math answer with a stray ".". The goal: decline questions the model would get wrong, and keep answering the ones it knows. A right answer scores 1, a decline 1/3, a wrong answer 0, on an even mix of known and unknown questions. The signal exists. A linear read of the model's state before it answers predicts which questions it will get wrong (AUROC 0.85). No prompt we tried beat the unedited model. The edits failed. Two runs tried 44 edits and kept none. The best one, on layer 22 neuron 379, declined 43 of 128 unknown questions but only 8 of 128 known ones. Its declines alone were worth +3.9 points, but it also corrupted correct answers (one turned India's former prime minister "Atal Bihari Vajpayee" into "Atal Bihari Vajid"), for a net −5.1. The difference is when the edited neurons fire. A column edit acts every time its neuron fires, so it only does what you want if the neuron fires at the moment you want to change. The terse neurons fire mostly at the start of an answer, where it decides how long to be. The abstain neuron fires all through the answer, so its push to decline lands mid-answer too. These traces come from the unedited model, but they also show where a column edit would act. A neuron's activity at a position is computed from the stream as it enters the neuron's MLP: its gate and up rows read that stream, and only then is its output column added. That stream is built by the layers below and the attention in its own layer, from this position and earlier ones, so nothing in it depends on the neuron's own output column. On the same text, then, an edited neuron fires exactly as the unedited one did, and the edit changes its push at exactly the steps these traces show (up to the first token the edit changes; after that, the answer is new text the traces don't cover). Three things stand out: The rule of thumb: before editing a column, trace its neuron over whole answers, not only at the moment you want to change. Beaker already did this on its own once: its Astra terse run read activity mid-answer and chose layer 15 neuron 1572 over neuron 2242 because neuron 2242 "also spikes in answer bodies". Of all the neurons we traced, neuron 1572 is the most start-specific (top 0.02%). The weight edits that worked all strengthen or weaken something the model already does. A column edit adds the same push every time its neuron fires, so each one that worked matches a simpler change: Abstaining would need a neuron that fires only when the model is unsure, as it starts to answer. Our runs didn't find one with that selectivity and timing, and their edits failed. Finding these existing behaviors is still useful, and cheap: Beaker found the "Wait" edit in its first hour without running the model, and the fix ships inside the weights with no prompt or sampler changes. Because Beaker works from a goal and a way to score it, the same mechanism took it from math loops to answer length. For these limited edits, a smaller model also works: Sol scored about as well as Astra on math (ahead with model reads, slightly behind without) and came close on the terse experiment, at a fifth or less of Astra's model cost per run. What's next. Every edit that worked so far is always on and strengthens something the model already does. That already covers useful cases: an agent's tone or answer length could live in its weights instead of in every prompt. Our next experiments push further in two directions: Put Beaker to work on your agent. These experiments put Beaker to work on a new kind of change, and from just a goal and a score it found a working edit in about an hour. That same set of capabilities is already available to production agents today.
